A defining strength of Orwell is its ethical focus. The game consistently challenges the player to reflect on the power they wield and the ease with which that power can be misused. Uploading information feels procedural and routine, yet the consequences are often deeply personal for the people affected. Careers are ruined, relationships collapse, and lives spiral based on decisions made in silence behind a terminal. The game does not present clear “right” answers; instead, it forces players to confront the reality that surveillance systems are shaped as much by human judgment and bias as by data itself. Visually, Orwell adopts a minimalist, utilitarian aesthetic that reinforces its themes. Interfaces resemble real-world operating systems and investigative software, grounding the experience in plausibility rather than spectacle. This stripped-down presentation keeps attention focused on text, decisions, and implications rather than visual distraction. Sound design is similarly restrained, using subtle cues rather than dramatic music to maintain an atmosphere of quiet tension and bureaucratic detachment. The result is an experience that feels unsettling precisely because of how ordinary and believable it is. Player agency is a key component of the experience, though it is intentionally constrained. While the overarching investigation follows a structured path, the specific outcomes depend heavily on what information you choose to reveal or withhold. Multiple endings and branching consequences encourage replayability, as players can explore how different ethical approaches alter the narrative. Some may approach the game as a dutiful analyst focused solely on public safety, while others may attempt to protect individual privacy whenever possible. Each approach reveals different facets of the story and reinforces the game’s central question: who decides what is justified when security and freedom collide? Reception to Orwell has been consistently positive, particularly among players who value narrative depth and social commentary. Many praise its relevance, especially in an era defined by data collection, algorithmic profiling, and online identity. While some may find the gameplay slow or limited due to its text-heavy nature, those willing to engage with its pacing often find it deeply immersive and emotionally resonant. The lack of traditional action is not a weakness but a deliberate design choice that underscores the quiet, insidious nature of surveillance. Ultimately, Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You stands as a powerful example of how games can explore modern societal issues with nuance and restraint. It transforms data analysis into a dramatic and morally charged experience, reminding players that information is never neutral and that those who control it shape reality itself. For players interested in narrative-driven games that challenge assumptions and provoke reflection rather than offer escapism, Orwell delivers a memorable and unsettling journey that lingers long after the screen goes dark. Rating: 8/10

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The premise is simple:
It's a game where you play a investigator who works for the government, sifting through data in all of its forms in order to fight for the safety of the public in the fictional world that it's set in.

There have been many 'hacking' games that have come out over the years, but Orwell takes the idea and puts you in the position of 'good' rather than 'bad', which creates the core ideology of the game -- If what you're doing is so good, then why do you feel so bad doing it?

The game proceeds along a UI of sorts, one that allows you to sift through websites, personal pages and even listen on some incredibly well-simulated 'real time chats', along with interruptions and intentional spelling errors that betray the typer's emotions and mental states. It's one of the best simulations of texting I've seen before in a game, and it DOES stand out. The articles and websites, while simple and clean, are detailed and packed full of worldbuilding -- the developers go out of their way to fill the world with detail that was never necessary to get from point A to B, but still fill everything with life and activity, and the world ends up feeling a little bit less compartmentalized than other games which force you into a limited POV.

However, this all leads back to the internal condundrum I have with this game:
You work with a handler who analyses the information you send him, and it's his job to make sense of it all. All you do is forward him the pertinent information, enough for him to make decisions and calls on how to handle situations. And you must choose what it is you want to send.

It's your choice to pick A over B. And it's not outright lies, because you're the good guy, remember? But whatever you send can tinge a thought, affect outcomes and colour perceptions in slight, yet pertinent, ways. Your own analysis plays a big part in how you want to portray someone else, and ultimately, the only one who has to live with the decisions you make is yourself.

Orwell is a great game about people, but more than that, it's a platform to help you examine yourself as a person. Since you're doing this for the percieved good, what decisions will you make and how far will you go to get what you want? And is there ever a time when personal freedom can be infringed upon for the greater result? Well... that might be another question for another time.

It's a good game tho, eh?

(( P.S.: Like any other 'visual novel' style game, and including the horrendous works of Mr. David Cage, I am fully aware that some of these 'choices' may be nothing more than illusionary. However, the game does it well enough in its context that reflecting upon the choices you make actually makes more than just a surface-level difference since you're playing not a character, but yourself. And considering the game's name and influences, I believe this to be the point. ))

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[i]Orwell[/i] is an episodic thriller involving the vulnerabilities of social media and easy access to critical digital information. You play as an employee of an NSA-like private government cyber-security agency called "Orwell", of course, named after George Orwell, and peep into your suspects' lives as you dig around for information that could tell if they are involved in anything that could put the lives of innocents in peril. The game is completely story-oriented, and at times, even choice-driven. 

[h1]Story:[/h1]

It's a thriller that follows the episode template like the [i]Telltale Games[/i], played as if you're a guy who's logged into his computer. Everything you do, see, or read is like as if you're logged into a computer. The story has a few interesting characters to read about, to peep into their lives and see just how much information you can dig up on them, and see how connected they are altogether. At times, you'll come across plot twists, and other kinds of ways the story could put you off with how you applied your actions by considering what you just saw right then first-hand, i.e., there may be more than meets the eye here. As the story progresses, the story gets deeper and darker, and your decisions will have to be considered more carefully. Sometimes, even the terms or choices given to you are there just to put you off. 

To me, I felt it drained down a bit when the whole plot unfolded, but it was pretty good overall. I haven't played the game extensively yet to see how many endings I could get, but there are indeed multiple endings. I don't dislike the endings that happen to you based on your choices. But the part of the story that you cannot change - the [b]huge[/b] plot twist - well, I didn't like it much. 

But more importantly, this game shows us just how exposed we are to everyone, and just how oblivious people are these days about this fact. It's pretty sci-fi, but who's to know that this could be our reality in a few years, give or take? We're slowly stumbling our way to a more surveilled future in which, you could say, we are going to live in an almost-communist digital world, where every singly word we type in the webs is taken for granted, and smeared on us as if we have anything troublesome to show for it. Hell, we go "Sorry, NSA" at times. So, in a way, we're just enjoying a false form of freedom. I could go into detail with how this is both good and bad, but this is only a game review, so... moving on. 

[h1]Visuals:[/h1]

The game looks like the people in it gave their own photos, and then they just used a heavily modified version of that Prisma app to convert it all to make it look like as it is. It's not bad. But, it kinda takes away the realism of it. I dunno if I could say it sits well with the tone of the game. I don't think it does. But, it's visually appealing. 

[h1]Mechanics & Gameplay:[/h1]

There's very little to no mechanics. Having the whole investigative thing in the game, it surely  calls for implementing the use of the keyboard. The devs could've considered adding search terms and stuff, but sadly, this mechanic wasn't added to the game, and that, too, takes away the realism from the game. Something like, if you can't find something in the game that you're looking for, that's related to a certain character, search the appropriate term up, and find it (like [i]Her Story[/i]). That's what would make it more engaging, because there's no knowing what you could possibly find. Clicking and dragging can get stale. Hopefully, if they make a follow-up to [i]Orwell[/i], they could implement this.

In the sense of gameplay, it's pretty interesting. As you play, you come across multiple choices to make. You're basically making choices constantly. When you have an info that you have the choice of either using it or not, you will probably think of the following:

"Do I drag this information to the profile?"
"[i]Should[/i] I drag this information to the profile?"
"How does this information have an effect?"
"Is this info even worth putting into the files?"

A simple statement that has to do something with the character - you will think it about in a much deeper manner. Because when you do enter something, it gets reflected on the reports, and that could have a cause-and-effect thing going on. The "choices matter" tag on this game is appropriate. And that's the whole point of the game. You, as an investigator, must see to it that everything you do in this works out perfectly in the end, for the people in Orwell, as well as the public.

[h1]Music:[/h1]

The music fits well with the theme of the game, it's sci-fi-y, it gives off the mysterious vibe, and if you see a plot twist, the music suddenly changes to a very tense, "oh damn" type of tone. 

[h1]Verdict:[/h1]

If all you do in a game is walk, then you call it a "walking simulator". This game is that. All you mostly do is click and drag stuff. Which makes it a "clicking simulator". But, it's appropriate, because you can't really do much with a computer other than click and drag and type, can you? 

Funny (lol, not) jokes aside, the premise of the game is solid, and how they elaborate on it, with you as the very thing that gets to use what's given to you against those [b]like[/b] us. Just imagine if this happened ([b][i]*cough*ishappening*cough*[/i][/b]) in real life. The primary focus of the game was definitely the story, and the story only. The replayability of the game relies on the achievements, and the multiple endings present in the game (for most, even trading cards).

I recommend this game to story lovers, I don't recommend this game to those who get bored of simple mechanics, and I recommend you get this game during the sales. I enjoyed the story a lot, but, I wanted more to do than just clicking and dragging. There's a [i]f-i-i-i-ne[/i] grey area between those two, and I'm right smack in the middle of it. But, being a game that focuses entirely on the story, and the kind of message it's trying to interpret to us, I give it a thumbs up.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A very interesting narrative experience that pulls you in quite well with busywork, much like Papers, Please. It has a very well-crafted and smooth user interface that could totally pass for a real spying program. The game gives you loads of freedom in how you selectively pass on information to alter the plot, and everything from what you choose to save to WHEN you choose to save it can affect the course of the story. At times, these flashpoints are signposted a little too hard, presumably to give players plenty of time to sort through the information at hand and come to a decision, but there are multiple instances when you have to make genunely DIFFICULT choices relying only on your intuition and the information you have gathered thus far. The game does not hold your hand about the consequences your actions will have.

However, the ending did feel a bit contrived and (while foreshadowed well enough), not terribly well justified. I know too well the amount of work that must have gone into such an involved branching story, but the game felt too short. Just when it was beginning to get difficult and the amount of information you had to deal with started to grow burdensome, the game ends. It feels a bit rushed out the door, and doesn't give you enough of a chance to play with the mechanics and start to really sweat. Ultimately, this reveals the underlying issue with Orwell: It is not a game. It is a moral lesson wrapped in an interactive experience. The developers had something they wanted to say, and so the game must come to an end so that they can say it.

I completed the 5-day story in 3-4 hours, but it has some replayability in going back to explore alternate outcomes if you had taken different paths. However, this robs the game of its magic; because you're making difficult decisions based on limited info, a blind playthrough adds a considerable amount. On your second playthrough, you're really just going through the motions to see what happens, which makes the leisurely pace at which characters interact torturous and tends to expose the man behind the curtain when you see how your choices DON'T affect the story.

It has several different endings, which are well-implemented, but the circumstances of the ending's gameplay were so muddled for me that I accidentally clicked my way into an ending I didn't want because I wasn't sure how to do what I wanted to do and I was loaded down with so much unprocessed information I had had to leave for later. The fact that the game jumps at the opportunity to end instead of letting you log out on your own terms when you've done what you want to do doesn't help. This critique probably makes more sense to those who have played it.

All in all, it's a brilliant little dystopia simulator with a lot of love and care poured into it, and a very pleasant and thought-provoking experience I highly recommend. Like any creation, it has its flaws, but it's well worth the price and you can tell how much work went into it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]TL:DR: [/b] Does 1984 ring a bell? Yes? You are all good, skip this. No? Block off four hours and prepare a lighthearted movie after to flush the existential horror.

[h1]What is Orwell?[/h1]
The player takes the role of an independent third party taking the reigns of the most powerful surveillance technology ever built tasked with the investigation of a terrorist attack on a monument in the capital of a fictitious country called The Nation. Armed with a context sensitive browser the player dives head first into one medium deep rabbit hole.

[h1]Game Design | The Awesome (+2)[/h1]
I adore the brutalist functionality of the game design. It feels like a desk job. There is nothing special to it. Everything works as one would expect it to. It should feel cold. It should provide a degree of separation from the subject while not hindering gameplay. This is one of the hardest tricks any game designer can pull off. Take it from a boring person who unironically loves to create spreadsheets for any number of things. This [i]rocks[/i].

[h1]Audio design | The Terrible (-2)[/h1]
Coming in on the opposite side of the spectrum is audio design. Or lack thereof. The only notable attempt at anything are dynamic music changes when the player comes across [i]shocking[/i] new information. And yes, I am exaggerating, because the music is exaggerating. The whiplash from the norm is that great. It arrives suddenly and leaves before it had a chance to order a frickin' latte. Then there are all the missed opportunities. The player has access to various types of data from texts, to web pages, to voice calls. Instead of a transcript it would have been great to have the few calls fully voiced. It would have brought the player even closer to the characters.

[h1]Characters | The Bad (-1)[/h1]
...of which Orwell utilizes several one dimensional archetypes with a couple of exceptions that show a hint of a second dimension. Fortunately for the game, the player is not forced to linger on any of the cast. We get just as much as we need to understand from where the wind is blowing before moving on to the next person. For better or worse, commentary on surveillance killing the human experience acts as the main character of the game and is largely responsible for the ankle deep depth of the human pawns.

[h1]Closing Thoughts | The Adequate (0)[/h1]
Orwell is a tricky proposition. On one side it is concise, excellently showcases pitfalls of absolute surveillance and should be a mandatory play on any high school, on the other side it is cynical to the core and does not allow a solution of the privacy/security conundrum. I could speculate that the original intention of the authors was to show the only winning move is not to play. However, I am writing this script seven years after the release in a world that is inching closer and closer to a world of AI driven absolute surveillance. The absolute surveillance of Orwell fails even with a human at the helm of its moral compass, what chance do we have in the real world without such an agent? At the end of the day art is a reflection of our perceived reality. I understand that having no way out nets a more chilling experience. However, if the resolution does not provide a positive outlook, something to aspire to, it leaves the observer in a very dark place.

[hr][/hr]

[h4]Note[/h4]
Individual sections (and the whole game) are critiqued on a scale of [i]The Terrible (-2)[/i] from the worse to [i]The Awesome (+2)[/i].

The only notable attempt at anything are dynamic music changes when the player comes across [i]shocking[/i] new information. And yes, I am exaggerating, because the music is exaggerating. The whiplash from the norm is that great. It arrives suddenly and leaves before it had a chance to order a frickin' latte. Then there are all the missed opportunities. The player has access to various types of data from texts, to web pages, to voice calls. Instead of a transcript it would have been great to have the few calls fully voiced. It would have brought the player even closer to the characters. [h1]Characters | The Bad (-1)[/h1] ...of which Orwell utilizes several one dimensional archetypes with a couple of exceptions that show a hint of a second dimension. Fortunately for the game, the player is not forced to linger on any of the cast. We get just as much as we need to understand from where the wind is blowing before moving on to the next person. For better or worse, commentary on surveillance killing the human experience acts as the main character of the game and is largely responsible for the ankle deep depth of the human pawns. [h1]Closing Thoughts | The Adequate (0)[/h1] Orwell is a tricky proposition. On one side it is concise, excellently showcases pitfalls of absolute surveillance and should be a mandatory play on any high school, on the other side it is cynical to the core and does not allow a solution of the privacy/security conundrum. I could speculate that the original intention of the authors was to show the only winning move is not to play. However, I am writing this script seven years after the release in a world that is inching closer and closer to a world of AI driven absolute surveillance. The absolute surveillance of Orwell fails even with a human at the helm of its moral compass, what chance do we have in the real world without such an agent? At the end of the day art is a reflection of our perceived reality. I understand that having no way out nets a more chilling experience. However, if the resolution does not provide a positive outlook, something to aspire to, it leaves the observer in a very dark place. [hr][/hr] [h4]Note[/h4] Individual sections (and the whole game) are critiqued on a scale of [i]The Terrible (-2)[/i] from the worse to [i]The Awesome (+2)[/i].

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is literally one of my favorite games of all time. As a point and click puzzle narrative adventure, the dystopian world it paints is really interesting. It puts you right in the seat of someone working within a government surveillance system, and the parallels to real life are chilling.

The game tackles the themes of government control and spying against there own people, in a way that feels both immersive and unsettling. You have to investigate people with almost no oversight, digging through chat logs, websites, and personal data, presented in beautifully designed 2D interfaces that feel just like the internet we use every day.

The gameplay revolves around finding and selecting highlighted bits of text. You decide which ones to submit, shaping the story as you go. This leads to multiple endings, where you can either side with the government or help those you're investigating. And, of course, there are tons of clever Easter eggs referencing the real Orwell.

It's a short but incredibly well crafted game, and I can’t recommend it enough.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The idea is excellent: You're an operative tasked with monitoring the social media and activities of various individuals suspected of or likely to carry out terrorist attacks, with the goal of stopping them. Initially, everything seems quite obvious and trivial, but it soon begins to explore gray areas and presents very interesting moral dilemmas.

After playing through it a couple of times, you become aware of the intricate plot and how linear it is, but during your first playthrough, it's practically imperceptible. It manages to create a strong sense of decision-making and truly draw you into its narrative. You genuinely feel like a spy because perhaps that's exactly what your job would look like if you were one. You would stop seeing people as individuals and begin to see them as pixels. That's the magic of Orwell.

The only important point to note is that it's heavily dependent on the language you speak. If the game isn't in a language you're fluent in, I recommend not playing it, as the game demands a lot from you in interpreting very specific data and dialogue, which could cause you to miss some excellent details that enhance the experience.
